extracted.intended_audience: life-science researchers and authors considering posting preprints
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for life-science researchers on what preprints are, their benefits and risks, server practices, impacts on journal review and priority, and how to share/advocate for preprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is a preprint
rubrics_metrics.description: A preprint is a scientific manuscript that is uploaded by the authors to a public server. The preprint contains data and methods, but has not yet been accepted by a journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most servers post the author's manuscript within a day or so without peer review; some servers perform brief quality-control inspections (see preprint server practices in the Preprint Server Directory). Preprints can be viewed (and possibly translated, reposted, or used in other ways, depending on the license) without charge by anyone in the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint content and licensing considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints contain data and methods and are posted by authors to a public server; posted manuscripts may be reused depending on the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be aware of the license applied to their preprint because it affects translation, reposting, and reuse. Servers vary in their license options and practices (see individual server pages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Server quality-control practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Some preprint servers perform brief quality-control inspections prior to posting; practices vary by server.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the Preprint Server Directory for details on individual servers' checks and policies. Brief QC does not replace formal peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versioning and permanence of preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Most preprint servers support versioning (posting updated versions of your paper based upon feedback and/or new data) and typically retain prior preprint versions which cannot usually be removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versioning allows authors to update manuscripts; retention of prior versions preserves the scholarly record and may limit removal of earlier content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprints and journal submission/integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Many preprint servers are integrated with one or more journals, making it possible to submit to both a server and a journal at once; preprint servers can also serve as a 'marketplace' for journal editors to invite submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the Preprint Server Directory for integrations. Examples: PLOS Genetics has 'preprint editors'; Proceedings of the Royal Society B has a preprint editorial team. Platforms like Review Commons allow posting refereed preprints that can be submitted to affiliate journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community commentary as a source of feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary on preprints (on the preprint site, social media, or platforms such as preLights, PREreview, or Peer Community In) can help authors improve their paper and may inform journal peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals and pilots consider community comments on preprint servers alongside traditional peer review. Authors can solicit and use such feedback to revise preprints prior to journal submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprints as a claim to priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints can establish priority of discovery because they have a time stamp, are publicly available, and are citable (arXiv in physics is cited as an example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While arXiv clearly establishes priority in physics, life-sciences practices vary; see discussions (e.g., Vale & Hyman) for community perspectives. Authors should consider preprints when they need a public timestamped disclosure of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of preprints on double-blind review
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints might make it more difficult to preserve blinding in double-blind peer review, since most servers do not enable anonymous posting and preprints increase early visibility of authors and work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COPE discourages pseudonymous preprint posting. Editors and referees should manage blinding carefully: referees are expected not to attempt to discover identities and to recuse themselves if they know the authors. Other public disclosures (seminar announcements, social media) also compromise blinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential negative consequences raised about preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns include: poor quality and irreproducible data being posted; rushing out premature data to claim priority; increased chance of scooping; and reporters or non-specialists using findings without recognizing interim status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ASAPbio notes there is no current evidence these problems worsen with preprints (drawn from arXiv history and biology preprints). Reputation incentives and community scrutiny can mitigate these risks; community may spot and correct poor work prior to journal publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprints and patent/public-disclosure implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints are considered public disclosure for the purposes of patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors who are pursuing patent protection should treat posting a preprint as a public disclosure that can affect patent rights and should consult patent counsel or institutional tech transfer offices before posting if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability and indexing of preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints are indexed in various discovery tools and repositories (examples: Europe PMC, Google Scholar, PrePubMed, OSF preprints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Europe PMC began indexing preprints in 2018; NCBI announced a pilot to include NIH-funded preprints in PubMed Central for certain topics (e.g., COVID-19). Authors can expect broad discoverability via multiple services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of preprinting (visibility, citations, feedback, scoop protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprinting increases visibility and citations, provides early constructive feedback, and most authors do not experience scooping problems after posting preprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited data: articles with a prior associated preprint receive 36% more citations; 37% of bioRxiv users reported receiving direct feedback via email; 99.3% of preprint authors reported no scooping problems. Use these potential benefits to weigh decision to preprint.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to support and advocate for preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals can advocate for preprints within their networks and join communities that support open science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical actions include sharing conference slides, using outreach materials (e.g., ASAPbio stickers), joining the ASAPbio community for learning/networking/leadership, and signing up for updates. Advocacy helps drive awareness and adoption locally.
